title: RECLAIM: Can Agents Reproduce the Claims of Machine Learning Papers?
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Sep 2026]
    Title:RECLAIM: Can Agents Reproduce the Claims of Machine Learning Papers?
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Reproducing a machine learning paper involves most research steps, from installing software and debugging to running experiments, work that AI agents increasingly do. We introduce RECLAIM, a benchmark of 100 NeurIPS 2025 papers that can be rebuilt yearly from new conferences. For each paper we fix in advance the result to reproduce, what counts as a successful reproduction, and a GPU-hour budget. An agent must reproduce that result using the paper and whatever its authors released. What the authors released decides the difficulty tier. Run-tier releases include code, data, and weights; Retrain-tier releases lack weights, so the agent trains the model; Reimplement-tier releases lack code, so the agent writes it. A separate language model grades runs from logs and outputs rather than agents' reports. We run four agents once per paper; the best agent in each tier reproduces only 41% of Run-tier papers, 27% at Retrain, and 15% at Reimplement, where every agent does worst. Failed attempts use on average 29% of their budget, so most stop with budget left. The most common agent error is writing the method without checking any part against the paper's numbers, in 63 of 400 runs.

report.summary: RECLAIM benchmarks whether AI agents can reproduce results from 100 NeurIPS 2025 papers, finding best agents succeed on only 15–41% depending on release completeness.
report.background: Machine learning has a reproducibility problem: papers often omit code, weights, hyperparameters, or compute details, so independent verification is expensive and slow. At the same time, AI agents are increasingly used to install software, debug, run experiments, and even write code, raising a natural question: can they autonomously reproduce published claims? RECLAIM addresses this by turning reproduction into a standardized benchmark. It uses 100 NeurIPS 2025 papers and fixes the target result, success criteria, and GPU-hour budget in advance, allowing yearly refresh with new conferences. Difficulty is set by what authors release, from full artifacts to paper-only descriptions, mirroring real-world conditions. The benchmark also separates execution from grading, using a language model to judge logs and outputs, not agent self-reports.
key_points: RECLAIM contains 100 NeurIPS 2025 papers and can be rebuilt yearly from new conferences. For each paper, the target result, success definition, and GPU-hour budget are fixed in advance, creating a controlled test of end-to-end reproduction rather than open-ended agent demos.

Difficulty depends on released artifacts. Run-tier includes code, data, and weights; Retrain-tier lacks weights, so the agent must train; Reimplement-tier lacks code, so the agent must write the method. This ladder separates engineering execution from genuine implementation.

Agent success is low. The best agent per tier reproduces only 41% of Run-tier papers, 27% at Retrain, and 15% at Reimplement. Reimplement-tier is hardest, showing that writing a correct method from a paper remains a major barrier.

Failures are not mainly due to exhausted compute. Failed attempts use on average 29% of their GPU-hour budget, so most stop with substantial budget remaining. This suggests poor planning, premature termination, or inability to diagnose failures rather than raw resource limits.

The most common error, in 63 of 400 runs, is writing the method without checking any part against the paper's numbers. Grading is done by a separate language model using logs and outputs, not agent reports, reducing self-assessment bias.
report.impact: The results temper expectations for fully autonomous AI research agents. For the AI industry, they highlight that reliable reproduction requires more than code generation: agents must read papers carefully, validate intermediate values, manage compute budgets, and debug failures. For developers, RECLAIM provides a concrete target for building verification-first agents, with opportunities in artifact discovery, experiment tracking, and automated error analysis. For regular users, the benchmark is a caution against trusting AI-generated research summaries or replication claims without evidence. It also points toward future tools that can check whether an AI agent actually reproduced a result, improving trust in AI-assisted science.
report.tools: To follow up, watch RECLAIM itself and related reproducibility/agent benchmarks such as PaperBench, MLAgentBench, CORE-Bench, and SWE-bench. Practical tooling includes Hugging Face Hub for models and datasets, DVC or Git LFS for data/code versioning, Weights & Biases or MLflow for experiment tracking, and Docker for environment capture. These help developers build agents that reproduce, verify, and report ML results.
